Hi Nora — great question. Short answer up front: cache hits are not billed for model compute; however they are accounted for against your commit in a specific way on committed plans. Details below so you can model both pay-as-you-go (PAYG) and commit scenarios.

1) PAYG (hosted API, no commit)
- If a response is served entirely from the prefix cache (exact match within TTL and same model variant), we do NOT charge model compute for the cached tokens. You will still see a small I/O/ingress/egress line on the invoice (negligible relative to compute) but there is no per-token compute charge for cached tokens.

2) Committed baseline (monthly/annual reserved tokens)
- For customers on a commit, cached responses are still considered for baseline usage accounting, but only when the cached response would otherwise have consumed compute on a cache miss. Practically that means cached tokens reduce your incremental PAYG compute usage, but they also decrement from your monthly baseline allocation when they fall into the same billing window and match the commit's model tier.
- We provide a separate "cache-eligible token" view in Console so you can see cache hits that consumed baseline vs. cache hits that were outside of baseline capacity.

3) Session vs. global prefix caches
- Session-scoped prefix cache (ephemeral per-user session) and global prefix cache (shared across requests for the same customer) behave the same for compute billing: if the returned output is an exact cached artifact we avoid compute charge. The difference is operational: global cache improves hit-rate across users and therefore is more likely to reduce overall compute spend.

4) Edge cases
- Partial hits (where the first N tokens are served from cache and the tail is generated): we only bill compute for the generated portion. Your token breakdown in Console will show both cached and generated token counts per request.
- TTL/consistency: a cached artifact must match the exact model + model revision + prompt/template + parameters (temperature, top_p, etc.) to be eligible. If you pin model revisions in rollouts, a revision bump invalidates previously cached artifacts for that model ID.

If you'd like, I can pull a sample 7-day run of your traffic and show projected savings across PAYG vs. a 12-month commit with a 30% cache hit rate. I've attached the updated ratecard for quick reference.

Nora — answers inline and I've looped in Vivek on the commit mechanics:

1) Baseline accounting for cached hits
- Yes: a cached response that would otherwise generate tokens deducts from your baseline one-for-one (so a 1,000-token cached response reduces the baseline by ~1,000 tokens). There is no additional compute charge, but it consumes baseline entitlement. The reasoning is that baseline is intended to cover your effective served output; we track served tokens (cached + generated) against the commit to keep billing transparent and predictable.
- Note: when customers want cache hits to be exempt from baseline consumption we can model that as a pricing exception for large buys — this is non-standard and would be applied contractually (example: certain knowledge-base-serving workloads where content is static and both parties agree to a cache-exempt clause).

2) Reporting CSV
- Console export supports the exact columns you mentioned: timestamp, request_id, project_id, model_id, model_revision, tokens_generated, tokens_cached, tokens_total, cache_ttl_seconds, cache_scope (session|global), charge_type (baseline|payg), and invoice_line_item_id. I'll attach a one-week sample CSV from a synthetic run so procurement can validate reconciliation (attached: atlas_usage_sample.csv).
